meta.text:
The internet is an important part of our daily lives. It helps people in many ways and makes communication easier.

One advantage of the internet is that it provides a lot of information. Students can use it to study, do research, and learn new skills. Another advantage is that it helps people communicate with friends and family through social media, emails, and video calls, even if they live far away.

However, the internet also has some disadvantages. People may spend too much time online, which can affect their health and reduce their time for study or exercise.

wrong:
فهم المقروء:
A queue that moves steadily feels shorter than a queue of the same length that stops and starts, even when the wait is identical. Research on waiting has produced a set of findings that are consistent enough to design around. Unoccupied time feels longer than occupied time, which is why mirrors near lifts and information screens in stations reduce complaints without reducing the wait. Uncertain waits feel longer than known ones: a sign saying the next train arrives in nine minutes is more tolerable than no sign at all, even when nine minutes is the longer wait. Unexplained waits feel longest of all, and an announcement giving a reason reliably lowers irritation. And people tolerate a long wait for something they value far better than a short wait for something they do not. None of this shortens anything. It is a reminder that the experience being managed is not the duration but the perception of it — and that the two can be improved separately.
What kind of wait feels longest?

فهم المقروء:
A queue that moves steadily feels shorter than a queue of the same length that stops and starts, even when the wait is identical. Research on waiting has produced a set of findings that are consistent enough to design around. Unoccupied time feels longer than occupied time, which is why mirrors near lifts and information screens in stations reduce complaints without reducing the wait. Uncertain waits feel longer than known ones: a sign saying the next train arrives in nine minutes is more tolerable than no sign at all, even when nine minutes is the longer wait. Unexplained waits feel longest of all, and an announcement giving a reason reliably lowers irritation. And people tolerate a long wait for something they value far better than a short wait for something they do not. None of this shortens anything. It is a reminder that the experience being managed is not the duration but the perception of it — and that the two can be improved separately.
What kind of wait feels longest?
